messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David was 25, but he felt much older, worn down by a vigilance that never ceased. He came to therapy after losing another job, this time as a housekeeper at a mid-range hotel. For years, the events of his childhood had been a tightly locked box, but now the lock was broken. The memories of his uncle, the dark basement closet, and the scratchy wool blanket were no longer contained. They bled into his days and owned his nights. The abuse had happened in darkness, often with the sound of his younger cousin crying in another room, a sound that had become a permanent fixture in David's own mind. The uncle would throw a coarse, foul-smelling blanket over him, and the texture of it against his skin is a sensation he can still conjure with perfect, sickening clarity.

His current life is a carefully constructed defense against these memories. Because he believes you can never know who will harm you, he is perpetually on guard, scanning faces, doorways, and shadows. This constant state of alert makes him acutely sensitive to his triggers. The sound of a child crying in the hotel corridor is enough to pull him back instantly. When a trigger hits, the memory returns not as a thought but as a full sensory reliving. Suddenly, he isn't in a hallway on the third floor; he is seven years old again, the rough wool scratching his cheek, the darkness absolute, his heart hammering against his ribs. He feels his body react before his mind can catch up, a cold sweat breaking out as he braces for a blow that isn't coming.

These moments are so overwhelming that his only recourse is to escape. He might drift off into a detailed fantasy world, a place he has built in his mind where he is safe and powerful, leaving his cleaning cart abandoned in the hallway. This retreat into his own world is one of the few strategies that offers temporary relief from the film of the event that plays over and over in his head. The memory itself reinforces his most deeply held fears about himself and the world. When it replays, it brings with it the sickening certainty that he is not a person but an object, something to be used and discarded. He feels this shame is visible on his skin, that guests and coworkers can see what happened to him just by looking at him, a belief that makes any social interaction an exercise in terror.

His strategies for survival have, over time, built a cage around him. Waking up in the dark is intolerable, sending a jolt of panic through him that demands immediate action. He lunges for the lamp, needing to flood the room with light. This fear dictates his living situation; he makes sure he is never alone, moving from one roommate to another, often straining relationships by insisting a light be left on all night. This constant avoidance has starved the memory of any chance to be processed or integrated. By refusing to be alone or in the dark, he ensures the memory remains frozen, pristine in its horror, ready to replay with full force the moment his guard slips.

The consequences of this cycle have been devastating. Each time he has to flee a situation or give up a responsibility—like abandoning a night shift he’d agreed to work—it cements the belief that he is fundamentally broken and exposed. He sees the proof of his dehumanization in every failed attempt at normalcy. He finally sought help after his most recent roommate, a friend from high school, told him he needed to move out. The prospect of having to find a new place, of potentially being alone, was more terrifying than the memories themselves. David now sits in the therapy room, quiet and watchful, afraid that he is beyond repair but holding onto a desperate hope that he might one day be able to stand in a dark room without feeling like he is about to be erased.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe how the trauma memory itself influences or sensitizes the patient to his triggers.
